Text: A toddler's and preschooler's lungs keep adding terminal bronchioles and alveoli, but the {{c1::musculature}} of those lungs is still poorly developed, so they cannot sustain {{c2::deep or rapid respirations::breathing pattern}} for long.
Back Extra:
Why: the extra terminal bronchioles and alveoli are being added to meet a growing body's ever-increasing oxygen demand.

Pitfall: the ceiling is muscular, not structural — a hard-breathing toddler runs out of power, not out of gas-exchange surface.

Text: In toddlers the loss of {{c1::passive immunity}} plus constant exposure to other children brings frequent viral colds, which often show up as {{c2::upper respiratory symptoms}} or {{c2::gastrointestinal distress}}. The antibodies those repeated infections generate become {{c3::acquired immunity}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the loss of passive immunity is called out as one of the most important physiologic changes of the toddler years, and it lands exactly when the child starts spending time around other children.

Distinguish: passive immunity is the protection the toddler is losing; acquired immunity is what replaces it.

Text: By the end of the preschooler stage (3 to 6 years), a child's brain weighs roughly {{c1::90%::percentage}} of its adult weight.
Back Extra: Cue: the preschool brain is nearly finished growing — the same stage in which play shifts from purely gross motor (grabbing an object with the whole palm) to fine motor (picking up a crayon with thumb and forefinger).

Text: Toddlers have the neuromuscular ability to control the bladder by {{c1::12 to 15 months::age range}}, but many are not psychologically ready for toilet training until {{c2::18 to 30 months::age range}}. On average, toilet training is complete at {{c3::28 months::age}}.
Back Extra:
Why: toilet training is the outward sign of renal-system maturation and the establishing of elimination patterns.

Cue: alongside speech development, it is one of the milestones by which a toddler wins the self-sufficiency at stake in the autonomy-versus-shame-and-doubt stage.

Text: Most children have mastered basic language skills by the age of {{c1::36 months::age}}, and understand full sentences by {{c2::3 or 4 years::age}}.
Back Extra: Cue: once the basics are in place, language stops being only a tool for asking for what they want and starts being used creatively and playfully.

Text: Toddlers begin to understand the concept of cause and effect at about {{c1::18 to 24 months::age range}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: cause-and-effect lands in the same stretch as this age group's social gains — becoming more interactive with other children is what teaches a toddler to control their own behavior, follow rules, and be competitive.

Ex: by observing their role models, toddlers of this age also learn to recognize gender differences.

Text: You are treating a severely injured child when the father, overwhelmed by fear, begins to panic and can no longer answer your questions. On this call the father has become a {{c1::secondary patient::role on scene}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: on any call for a severely sick or injured child, look for the second patient on scene — a parent.

Pitfall: the parent's distress adds to an already intense situation and makes the task of treating the child much more difficult.

Text: Each year a school-age child (6 to 12 years) gains about {{c1::4 pounds (2 kg)::weight}} and grows about {{c2::2.5 inches (6 cm)::height}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the same 6-to-12 stretch also swaps baby teeth for permanent teeth and brings a significant rise in brain activity in both hemispheres.

Text:
School-age children develop moral reasoning in three levels, each answering to a different influence:

{{c1::Preconventional}} → {{c2::external forces such as parental discipline}}

{{c1::Conventional}} → {{c2::the approval of peers and society}}

{{c1::Postconventional}} → {{c2::an internalized moral compass (conscience)}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: under preconventional reasoning an act is right or wrong by its consequences — punishment or incentive. Conventional reasoning still accepts the rules of authority figures, but now because those rules are seen as necessary for positive relationships and acceptance. Postconventional reasoning turns abstract and answers to conscience alone.

Cue: the order tracks who is in charge — the punisher, then the group, then the self. Postconventional reasoning keeps developing through adolescence.

Text: {{c1::Self-concept}} is {{c2::our perception of ourselves}}, whereas {{c1::self-esteem}} is {{c2::how we feel about ourselves}} and how we fit in with our peers.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: self-concept is the picture you hold of yourself; self-esteem is the verdict on that picture.

Cue: both begin to take shape during the school-age years, the same stage in which the three levels of moral reasoning develop.
